title: K Lab Product Ecosystem
summary: Built a shared component library and scalable front-end architecture that unified eight fintech applications, streamlined development, and established a consistent product experience.

hero.alt: Shared fintech product interfaces and design tokens on a desktop display

text: K Lab was developing a growing suite of fintech applications, each addressing different business workflows and operational needs.
I led UI/UX and front-end development across the ecosystem, creating both the visual design system and the underlying reusable development infrastructure.

At the center was a shared React component library, distributed as an npm package with CLI-based installation, allowing developers across K Lab to integrate standardized components and application patterns into their projects.
My responsibilities included product UX, component architecture, front-end implementation, technical planning, and leading a small development team.
As K Lab's product suite expanded, applications had inconsistent interfaces, navigation patterns, and interaction models.
Developers were repeatedly implementing similar functionality across separate codebases, creating duplicated effort and making consistent updates more difficult.
The challenge extended beyond visual consistency. We needed a reusable development foundation that could:

items: Simplify the implementation of common functionality.
Allow developers to install and reuse components across independent applications.
Remain flexible enough for different product requirements.

sections.heading: Build once. Install anywhere. Extend as needed.

text: Rather than treating the design system as a collection of Figma assets, I approached it as a shared product development platform.
The goal was to give developers a consistent starting point without limiting their ability to customize components for specific applications.

items.title: Design tokens

items.title: Component library

items.title: CLI installation
items.body: A streamlined way to install components and accelerate adoption.

items.title: Application patterns

sections.heading: More than a design system.
sections.lede: The component library became a reusable development foundation shared across K Lab applications.

text: It evolved through several levels of abstraction. This approach connected UI/UX design decisions directly to implementation, making consistency an architectural feature rather than a manual design exercise.

items.title: UI primitives
items.body: Buttons, inputs, dialogs, cards, form controls, and other foundational components.

items.title: Composite components
items.body: More sophisticated components combining multiple primitives into reusable interactions.

items.title: Application-level patterns
items.body: Complete interface structures and workflows, including authentication and login layouts, application launch pages, navigation and sidebar systems, data tables with filtering, search, pagination, and actions, and support interfaces.

items.title: Distribution and developer experience
items.body: Packaging and CLI-based installation enabled developers to bring components into different application codebases without rebuilding them.

text: AI-assisted development became part of my workflow for planning, implementation, refactoring, and iteration.
This helped a small UI and front-end team work across a broad product ecosystem while keeping architectural decisions, UX quality, and implementation standards human-led.

text: The project established shared design and front-end development infrastructure across K Lab's eight-application ecosystem.

items: An installable React component library distributed through npm and a CLI.
Reusable components and complete application-level patterns.
Reduced need to repeatedly implement common UI functionality.
More consistent navigation, styling, and interactions.
A more standardized developer experience across applications.
A maintainable foundation for future product development.

blocks.title: Takeaway
blocks.body: The most valuable outcome wasn't an individual interface. It was building a reusable system that connected design and engineering, allowing developers to create consistent product experiences without starting from scratch.
